2027-04-03.title: Saturday within the Octave of Easter
readings: We cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard
I praise you, Lord, for you have answered me (or: Alleluia)
Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation
2027-04-03.alt: Day within the Octave of Easter, kept with the rank of a solemnity. The Gloria is sung; the Easter Sequence may be sung before the Gospel acclamation; the dismissal has the double Alleluia. Liturgical colour: white. First Saturday of the month. Ninth and last day of the Divine Mercy Novena. Those who wish to gain the plenary indulgence of Divine Mercy Sunday may go to confession today (sacramental confession within about twenty days before or after is sufficient).
2027-04-03.verse: And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.”
theo: The council looks at Peter and John and is puzzled. These are not scholars trained in the law; they are “uneducated and ordinary men,” fishermen from Galilee. Yet they speak with a boldness that cannot be explained by learning. Then the leaders understand where it comes from: they “recognized them as companions of Jesus.” Time spent with Jesus had left its mark. And there is something they cannot argue against: “When they saw the man who had been cured standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition.” A man who had never walked now stands in the middle of the court. So they send the Apostles out and talk among themselves: “What will we do with them? For it is obvious to all who live in Jerusalem that a notable sign has been done through them; we cannot deny it.” Their only plan is to stop the news from spreading: “let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.”

Peter and John give an answer that has inspired Christians in every age of persecution: “Whether it is right in God's sight to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge; for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard.” They are respectful; they do not insult the council or stir up the crowd. But they will not be silent about the truth. They have seen the Risen Lord; they have heard his voice; to keep quiet would be to deny what is real. The leaders threaten them again and let them go, because “all of them praised God for what had happened.” The Psalm gives the Apostles' song of victory: “The LORD is my strength and my might; he has become my salvation.” And, from the lips of the risen Christ himself: “I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD.” The Church is bound to obey lawful authority in all that is just; but when any power commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, the Christian must answer as Peter did.

The Gospel is taken from the ending of St Mark, a short summary of the Easter appearances. Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, “from whom he had cast out seven demons.” She goes and tells the disciples, who are “mourning and weeping,” but “they would not believe it.” He appears “in another form” to two of them walking into the country, the Emmaus disciples, and again “they did not believe them.” At last he appears to the Eleven at table, “and he upbraided them for their lack of faith and stubbornness, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen.” It is a surprisingly honest page. The first witnesses of the Resurrection were not credulous people looking for a miracle; they were slow, sad and hard to convince. That is why their faith, once it came, is so trustworthy.

And then, to these very men who had doubted, Jesus entrusts the whole world: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.” He does not wait for perfect disciples. He sends the forgiven, the slow of heart, the ones who were rebuked a moment earlier. The two readings meet here: the Apostles who once would not believe are now the ones who “cannot keep from speaking.” The Octave of Easter ends tomorrow, but its message is just beginning. The Collect prays that God, who gives increase to the peoples who believe, may clothe the newly baptized with blessed immortality. In ancient Rome the neophytes wore their white baptismal garments all through this week and laid them aside at the end of it; the white garments were put away, but the life of Christ they signified was meant to be carried into every street and home.
conn: The Greek agrammatoi and idiōtai mean men without formal rabbinic training and private persons without office, not that they could not read. The council was surprised that such men spoke so well.
Literally, “they had been with Jesus.” Mark 3:14 says Jesus chose the Twelve first “to be with him,” and then to be sent out to proclaim.
The word parrēsia, freedom and courage of speech, runs all through Acts (4:13, 29, 31; 28:31). It is a gift of the Holy Spirit.
Obeying God rather than human beings.

Peter repeats this principle in Acts 5:29. The Catechism teaches that citizens are obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the moral order or the Gospel (CCC 2242).

Mark 16:9–20 is missing from some of the oldest Greek manuscripts and differs in style from the rest of the Gospel. It was known in the second century and is part of the canonical Scriptures received by the Church as inspired (Council of Trent, 1546).
All four Gospels place her at the empty tomb; Mark and John say the Risen Lord appeared to her first. The Church calls her “apostle of the apostles,” and since 2016 her day (22 July) is a feast.
Mark's brief allusion to the Emmaus story (Luke 24:13–35), when the two disciples did not at first recognize the Lord.

In the early Church the newly baptized wore white garments throughout Easter week and laid them aside at the end of the Octave; hence the old Latin names of this Saturday and of tomorrow's Sunday, “in albis.”
altar: The Apostles spoke so boldly because they had been with Jesus. Every Mass is time spent with him: the same Lord who sat at table with the Eleven sits at table with us and gives himself to us in the Eucharist.

At the end of Mass we hear “Go forth,” with the double Alleluia. It is a small echo of the Lord's command: go into all the world. We do not leave the altar to go home only; we leave it to take the good news with us.

live: Give fifteen minutes today to silent prayer before the Blessed Sacrament or with the Gospel.
Go to confession today if you can, and finish the Divine Mercy Novena tonight.
If you are asked to keep silent about what is true and right, at work or among friends, answer respectfully but do not deny the truth.
On this First Saturday, pray the Regina Caeli and a decade of the Rosary in reparation and thanksgiving.
fathers: St Gregory the Great (Homily 29 on the Gospels, in substance)

The disciples were slow to believe the Resurrection, and this was not so much their weakness as our future strength. By their doubts, healed by so many proofs, our faith is made firm. And when the Lord says “to the whole creation,” he means the human being, who shares being with the stones, life with the plants, feeling with the animals and understanding with the angels.
St John Chrysostom (Homilies on Acts 10, in substance)

See how the uneducated put the learned to silence. The rulers came with their power and their threats; the fishermen had only the truth and the name of Jesus, and it was the rulers who were at a loss.
St Bede the Venerable (On Mark, in substance)
The Lord rebuked the hardness of his disciples at table so that, once corrected, they might preach with greater confidence to others what they themselves had come to believe through so many signs.
magis: The disciples' doubts show that the Resurrection was not the product of their faith or credulity; their faith was born of the encounter with the Risen One.
The missionary mandate: the Church is sent by Christ to proclaim the Gospel to every creature.
Citizens must not follow directives of civil authority that are contrary to the moral order: we must obey God rather than men.
Every baptized person is a missionary disciple; we do not need long training to tell others of the love of God we have met.
The books of Scripture, with all their parts, are inspired by the Holy Spirit and have God as their author.
saints: Bishop of Chichester in England (1197–1253), commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 3 April. A humble and generous pastor, remembered for the prayer: may I know you more clearly, love you more dearly, and follow you more nearly, day by day.

4 Apr: Second Sunday of Easter, Sunday of Divine Mercy, Octave Day of Easter. 5 Apr: the Annunciation of the Lord (transferred from 25 March), with Gloria and Creed. 7 Apr: St John Baptist de la Salle.
2027-04-03.prayer: O God, who by the abundance of your grace give increase to the peoples who believe in you, look with favour on those you have chosen and clothe with blessed immortality those reborn through the Sacrament of Baptism. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, you were patient with disciples who were slow to believe, and you sent them into all the world. Keep us close to you, so that people may see that we have been with you; give us the courage of Peter and John, and let us never keep silent about what we have seen and heard. Alleluia. Amen.

2027-04-03.question: Would anyone who watched me this week guess that I have been with Jesus?
catechism: The doubts of the disciples and the reality of the Resurrection.
kidsaint: Richard was a bishop in England who loved the poor. He gave away so much that his helpers worried there would be nothing left! He wrote a little prayer: dear Jesus, help me to know you more clearly, love you more dearly and follow you more nearly, day by day. Lesson: we can pray Richard's prayer every morning.

term: A Greek word for freedom and courage in speaking, especially speaking the truth before the powerful. In Acts it is a gift of the Holy Spirit to the Apostles and to all who witness to Jesus.

family.explain: The leaders told Peter and John: stop talking about Jesus! But Peter and John said: we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard. They had seen Jesus alive, and they were so happy that they had to tell everyone.
family.intention: We pray for Christians who are not allowed to speak about Jesus, that God may give them courage and keep them safe.
family.ask: Ask: “What is the best thing we know about Jesus?” Choose together one person to tell this week.

illus: A young clerk in a bank in Thrissur was told by his manager to change a date on a loan record so that a powerful customer could avoid a penalty. He said politely that he could not do it. The manager was angry, and within months the clerk was transferred to a small branch far from home. Two years later an audit found the old irregularities, and the manager was removed. The clerk's mother said only: you obeyed God, and he did not forget you. It is a small story, but it is the same answer Peter gave: whether it is right to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, risen from the dead, let us be with you now, and fill us with the boldness of your Holy Spirit. Alleluia. Amen.
share: They recognized them as companions of Jesus (Acts 4:13). What in my life shows that I have been with Jesus?
We cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard (Acts 4:20). What have I seen and heard of God that I keep to myself?
Go into all the world (Mark 16:15). Where is my little part of the world?
pm.resp: I praise you, Lord, for you have answered me.
interc: For Christians who suffer for their faith, that they may have the courage of Peter and John.
For those in authority, that they may never command what is against God's law.
For all who are slow to believe, that the Risen Lord may be patient with them as with the Eleven.
For the newly baptized of this Easter, that they may keep the white garment of grace unstained.
For our group, that we may finish the Divine Mercy Novena with faith and prepare well for tomorrow.
pm.close: Father, you sent your Son's disciples into all the world. Make us faithful companions of Jesus and joyful messengers of his good news. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, the leaders look at Peter and John and see ordinary men, fishermen without formal training. Yet they speak with a boldness that astonishes everyone. And the leaders understand: they had been with Jesus (Acts 4:13).

That is the secret of every true witness. Not cleverness, not money, not position, but time spent with Jesus. If we pray, read the Gospel and come to Mass, people will see it in our faces and hear it in our words.

The council orders them never again to speak in the name of Jesus. Peter and John answer: whether it is right in God's sight to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge; for we cannot keep from speaking about what we have seen and heard (Acts 4:19–20). They are respectful, but they will not deny the truth.

The Gospel tells us something surprising. The Eleven did not believe Mary Magdalene. They did not believe the two disciples from Emmaus. When Jesus came, he upbraided them for their lack of faith and stubbornness (Mark 16:14). The Apostles were not easy believers. Their faith was won by the Risen Lord himself.

And yet, to these same slow disciples, Jesus says: go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation (Mark 16:15). He does not wait until we are perfect. He sends us as we are, forgiven and loved.

Tomorrow is Divine Mercy Sunday. Today is a good day to make a good confession and finish the novena. Let us ask for the grace to be with Jesus, so that we too cannot keep from speaking of him. Alleluia. Amen.
